transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-20
Time: 15:21 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (EmeraldTech Eng), Marco Lee (EmeraldTech SRE), Dana Ortiz (EmeraldTech Head of ML), Liam O'Rourke (EmeraldTech Security)

Summary: quick console walkthrough focused on trace correlation, KV cache fallbacks, error escalation, and candidate rollout strategies. Customer wants a reproducible runbook for debugging failures tied to request ids, plus a proposal for a short pilot to validate latency and cost under realistic traffic.

Topics covered:
- Request-level traces and stitching across microservices
- Request playback and reproducing error paths
- KV cache misses and fallback to larger model variants
- Audit logs, SSO and KMS integrations
- Next steps: benchmarking pilot, security doc share, pricing follow-up

Transcript:
[00:00] Jared: alright everyone thanks for joining, we got about an hour, i can kick off with a short agenda. is that okay?
[00:05] Priya: yup, sounds good. dana and i will mostly watch for the ML constraints, marco's going to dig into ops questions.
[00:12] Jared: perfect. so goal today is a console walkthrough — request tracing, error analysis, and how you can use playbacks to reproduce bad paths. sofia, wanna take it away on the trace inspector?
[00:18] Sofia: yeah, i'll share screen — okay, i'm on the Conductor Console home, quick note, i might say "K-V cash" sometimes, that's the transcription in the logs but it's KV cache. so first view is the request table, you can filter by model, route, status codes, and correlation id. i've got a demo trace from last week that shows a cascade: user request -> preprocessing service -> embedder -> redwood runtime, then a cache miss and fallback.
[00:42] Priya: can you show the raw request payload please? we want to ensure prompt redaction and pii handling.
[00:46] Sofia: yep, payload view has automatic redaction flags — we show tokens that were redacted and why. there is a toggle to reveal for users with proper RBAC.
[00:55] Marco: how long do you keep raw request logs in hosted? our compliance team wants 30 days max, and anonymized indexes after that.
[01:00] Jared: hosted default is 90 days, enterprise customers can configure retention and we support archiving to customer S3/VPC endpoints or export to SIEM. for private deployments you control retention fully.
[01:12] Liam: and encryption? keys at rest? we use HSM and want KMS integration.
[01:18] Sofia: yes, support for customer-managed KMS/HSM; the private plane — sorry private control plane — integrates with your KMS for secrets and we encrypt logs at rest.
[01:26] Priya: show a trace timeline, specifically where the model fallback happened.
[01:30] Sofia: ok, timeline mode — here's the request's span tree. you can expand the runtime span to see token-level latencies and kv cache hit/miss metadata. here you see an initial cache miss at token 0 and then a fallback route triggered to the 8-bit quantized variant. the console records the exact model id, kernel variant, and the reason code: "kv_miss_size_exceeded".
[01:55] Marco: we occasionally see degraded outputs after fallback, is there a way to tie prompt sets to quality regressions?
[02:00] Sofia: yes, the console links to the Optimize panel where you can tie prompt sets/evals to model versions. we can show a regression alert that flags a change when moving to scaled quantized variants. it surfaces sample prompts that failed thresholds.
[02:14] Dana: quick clarifying q: when you say "fallback to 8-bit", is that automatic? can we configure thresholds?
[02:20] Jared: automatic by default but fully configurable — you can set SLOs (latency/cost thresholds) and whether fallback is allowed for a particular route or tenant. for high-quality routes you can pin to a single variant and disable fallback.
[02:33] Priya: how is the downstream service correlation performed? we have a proprietary orchestrator — we need to stitch traces from our side.
[02:39] Sofia: we accept custom correlation headers and can ingest trace ids from your orchestrator. the tracer normalizes and stitches using a best-effort algorithm; sometimes ids get munged and the UI will show partial matches flagged as "probable stitch".
[02:52] Marco: we saw an earlier call transcript example where the header was stripped by a CDN, producing orphan spans. can the console backfill?
[02:58] Sofia: we can backfill using request logs and prefix keys — but there's a best effort; we also provide a small sidecar library for guaranteed propagation.
[03:08] Priya: can you demo request playback? we want to reproduce an error path end-to-end.
[03:12] Sofia: sure — playback mode spins up a sandboxed runner that replays the exact recorded inputs against a pinned model variant. i can select the request id and run it. note: playback will honor your RBAC and won't leak secrets.
[03:25] [screen click noises]
[03:31] Sofia: the playback shows token deltas, timings, and any divergences. here's a case where the behavior diverged because the runtime selected a different kernel due to sequence length threshold. it gives a diff of the outputs and marks the earliest mismatch.
[03:50] Dana: interesting. can playback be run in our VPC? we need to run benchmarks in our network to get realistic latencies.
[03:56] Jared: yes, for Private deployments playback runs inside your VPC. for Dedicated we can offer a sandbox runner in a dedicated cluster in your account.
[04:06] Marco: latency vs cost: if we pin to high-precision models we'll hit 4x cost. what levers do we have?
[04:12] Sofia: batching, KV caching, and quantization profiles. the Optimize tab will recommend the most cost-effective quantization and batching config for your traffic patterns, and show estimated per-token cost impact. also smart routing can move low-latency requests to hosted cheaper variants and high-quality ones to dedicated low-latency pools.
[04:29] Priya: show an example of an alert when a route degrades.
[04:33] Sofia: alerts are threshold based and tied to a route. here's an alert that fired when p95 latency crossed 350ms and output quality dropped on the eval set. it auto-created an incident with the top correlated traces and assigned it to the on-call.
[04:46] Priya: nice. on incident postmortems, do you store the trace playbacks for audit?
[04:50] Jared: yes we snapshot playbacks and preserve anonymized replays for the incident timeline; for enterprise we can export to your long-term archive.
[04:58] Marco: about RBAC — can we restrict who can reveal redacted fields in the console?
[05:02] Sofia: yes, fine-grained RBAC, SSO via SAML/Okta, and audit logs for all reveal actions.
[05:10] Liam: couple security items: 1) we require MFA + SSO enforced for admin roles; 2) need a listing of subprocessor locations for data residency; 3) we want to run a threat model review.
[05:20] Jared: we'll share the compliance pack and the subprocessor list, and schedule a short security review with our security engineering.
[05:28] Priya: moving back to debugging flows — can we annotate traces and assign owners within the console?
[05:33] Sofia: yes, you can add comments, tag spans, and assign to users; comments persist on the trace and show up in the incident timeline.
[05:40] Dana: how do you handle multi-tenant isolation? our product serves multiple clients and we need strong separation.
[05:46] Jared: dedicated tenants get isolated GPU pools and separate runtime instances; private deployments are fully customer-managed. we also support namespace-based RBAC and strict tenancy controls in the hosted offering.
[05:58] Marco: okay, quick technical deep dive — why do KV cache misses spike when sequence length distribution changes?
[06:04] Sofia: typically because the cache key includes sequence-length-normalized prefixes; if users start sending longer contexts the KV key changes and hits drop. our runtime supports prefix normalization and we can surface the distribution in the console so you can tune the cache key strategy.
[06:20] Priya: can you show the distribution plot?
[06:23] Sofia: sure — here's a histogram of request lengths and the associated hit rate. you can click on a bin and get sample traces. see that long-tail bin with 2% of requests causing a 30% drop in hit rate — that's often the culprit.
[06:40] Marco: for the pilot we want a script to simulate our traffic including the long-tail. can you provide that?
[06:45] Sofia: yes, i'll attach a synthetic workload script and a notebook that runs on your infra.
[06:50] Jared: action: sofia will share benchmark notebook and workload script, i'll send the pricing sheet, liam will send compliance questions.
[06:58] Priya: one last question — how do you surface fallback-induced quality regressions to product folks?
[07:03] Sofia: we create regression alerts tied to eval prompt sets and push examples into Slack/Teams channels; the Optimize dashboard also shows per-route quality delta over time.
[07:12] Dana: ok thanks, this is useful. let's schedule the pilot next week.
[07:16] Jared: great, i'll poll for availability and send calendar invites.
[07:20] Marco: agreed, i'd like the pilot to include a run against our staging VPC with the playback runner.
[07:25] Jared: noted. returning to the transcript, i want to highlight three takeaways: 1) we can reproduce the error path with playback and it surfaces kernel-level diffs; 2) caching/sequence-length normalization will likely fix your hit-rate drop; 3) we can run a two-day pilot to validate latency and cost with a follow-up sizing meeting.
[07:45] Priya: that's accurate. thanks everyone.
[07:49] Dana: thanks.
[07:51] Jared: closing, will send notes, pricing, and security pack.
[07:55] End of meeting.
